COMPLETE EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Method: Two-stage least squares (Instrumental-Variables).  

Why IV?  
• The treatment—number of slaves exported from an ethnic homeland—is continuous and was not randomly assigned.  
• We observe only one “post-treatment” cross-section (contemporary economic outcomes), so difference-in-differences or event-study designs are infeasible.  
• Geographic determinants of slave capture and transport costs are plausibly exogenous to subsequent economic trajectories and can be used as instruments.  
• IV tackles the two main empirical concerns: (i) omitted historical factors that co-vary with slave exports and modern outcomes, and (ii) attenuation bias from measurement error in historical counts.  

Candidate instruments (Zᵢ):  
a) Great-circle distance from ethnic-group centroid to the nearest major slave-export port on the Atlantic or Indian Ocean.  
b) Directional “wind‐cost” index (based on prevailing currents and winds between each homeland and the nearest port).  
c) Terrain ruggedness along the optimal overland path to the port (impacts capture/transport cost but not modern GDP except through slave exports).  
We will use the first principal component of (a)–(c) to maximize first-stage strength or stack them in an over-identified system and report Hansen tests.  

================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable Tᵢ  = ln(1 + total slaves exported 1400–1900 per 1,000 people in ethnic homeland i).  

Control/comparison: Ethnic groups with lower or zero recorded exports (continuous treatment; control is effectively the lower tail of the distribution).  

Timing: Treatment occurred historically between 1400–1900; outcome is measured circa 2000-2020 (latest GDP per capita, night-lights density, household asset indices).  

================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Instrument relevance: Geographic-cost variables strongly predict variation in slave exports.  
• Plausible—distance, winds, and ruggedness all affected traders’ marginal costs.  
A2. Exclusion restriction: Conditional on historical covariates and geography controls, the instruments affect today’s economic development only through their impact on historical slave exports.  
• Credible because the instruments capture 15th–19th-century transport technology; any remaining direct channel (e.g., coastal proximity affects modern trade) is controlled for with modern transport-access controls (distance to coast, roads, ports).  
A3. Independence: Instruments are as-good-as-random with respect to unobserved pre-slavery determinants of long-run development.  
• We will control for baseline agro-climatic potential, pre-1500 population density (from Hyde), and continental fixed effects (Atlantic vs Indian Ocean catchment).  
A4. Monotonicity: Groups further from ports (higher-cost side of the instrument) could not have been more exposed to slaving than closer groups, other things equal.  
• Plausible: transport cost raises, not lowers, extraction.  
A5. SUTVA: Slave extraction from one group does not directly alter the potential outcome of another except through aggregate general-equilibrium effects, which are small at ethnic-homeland scale.  

================================================================  
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Threat 1: Post-treatment migration/ethnic-border changes → mis-measurement of who was “treated.”  
• Mitigation: Use historical homeland polygons from Murdock (1959) rather than today’s administrative borders; replicate analysis with modern survey clusters aggregated back to historical homelands; conduct robustness drop for homelands with large inward migration during colonial period.  

Threat 2: Coastal access is both an instrument component and a direct driver of modern development.  
• Mitigation: Include controls for straight-line distance to coast, distance to nearest modern port, malaria ecology, and climatic suitability. Also run “exclusion-modified” specifications that residualize instruments on modern coast-distance so only variation orthogonal to coast remains.  

Threat 3: Measurement error in historical slave counts (attenuation + misclassification).  
• Mitigation: (i) log-plus-one transformation; (ii) IV corrects attenuation; (iii) use multiple data sources (Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, Indian Ocean voyages) and average; (iv) conduct SIMEX-style sensitivity to alternative noise levels.  

================================================================  
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # OLS & IV regressions
library(modelsummary) # clean tables
library(stargazer)    # optional reporting

# 1. Load data -----------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("slave_trade_ethnic_data.csv")  # main file
# expected columns:
# ethnic_id, slaves_total, pop_1400, gdp_pc_2015,
# dist_port_km, wind_cost, path_rugged,
# coast_dist_km, pre1500_popdens, agro_pot

# 2. Construct variables -------------------------------------
dt[, ln_slaves_pc := log1p(slaves_total / pop_1400 * 1000)]
dt[, gdp_log := log(gdp_pc_2015)]
# instruments
dt[, Z1 := log(dist_port_km)]
dt[, Z2 := wind_cost]
dt[, Z3 := log1p(path_rugged)]
# PCA (optional)
#library(FactoMineR); pca <- PCA(dt[, .(Z1,Z2,Z3)], scale.unit=TRUE, ncp=1)
#dt[, Zhat := pca$ind$coord[,1]]

# 3. Baseline 2SLS -------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- gdp_log ~ ln_slaves_pc + coast_dist_km + agro_pot + pre1500_popdens | 
                        coast_dist_km + agro_pot + pre1500_popdens + Z1 + Z2 + Z3

est_main <- feols(iv_formula, data = dt, cluster = ~ethnic_id)
etable(est_main, se = "cluster")

# 4. Robustness: Alternative instrument = distance only -------
iv2 <- gdp_log ~ ln_slaves_pc + coast_dist_km + agro_pot + pre1500_popdens |
                  coast_dist_km + agro_pot + pre1500_popdens + Z1

est_alt <- feols(iv2, data = dt, cluster = ~ethnic_id)

# 5. Robustness: Oster bounds (if needed) ---------------------
# library(psacalc) or perform manual delta; omitted for brevity.

# 6. Summarize results ---------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(Main = est_main, AltDist = est_alt),
             statistic = "conf.int",
             stars = TRUE)
```

================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic theory and the qualitative historical record suggest that large-scale slave extraction weakened local institutions, reduced social trust, and suppressed human-capital accumulation. I therefore expect:  
• Direction: Negative.  
• Magnitude (1st-stage SD): A one standard-deviation increase in ln(slaves per capita) (~≈ 0.9) will lower current log-GDP per capita by roughly 0.15–0.25 log points (≈ 15–25 %).  

================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Instrument strongly predicts treatment (F-stat > 10)…………… 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction plausibly holds…………………………… 0.8  
C3: Independence from unobservables…………………………………… 0.7  
C4: Monotonicity / no defiers…………………………………………… 1  
C5: SUTVA (no cross-unit interference)………………………………… 0.8  
Average ≈ 0.86 → generally credible, though exclusion and independence warrant careful discussion and robustness tests.
